subtopic: STATEMENT OF MR. MACKENZIE KING WITH REFERENCE TO REPORT IN TORONTO GLOBE AND MAIL OF MARCH 31

speechtext:
Right Hon, W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):	At last night's sitting I
drew attention to an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of March 31, under the name of Mr. Harold Dingman. staff writer of the Globe and Mail, which I felt affected the privileges of this house, inasmuch as it contained a statement which was attributed to me, which was not in accordance with the statement I made in this house, and which as published was certain to create an entirely erroneous impression as to the significance and actual meaning of what I had said.
After the house rose last night the publisher of the Globe and Mail, in company with Mr. Dingman, came to my office and explained to me the circumstances which accounted for the article containing the passage to which I had taken exception, and stated that Mr. Dingman himself was in no way responsible for the particular paragraph that appeared in the article under his name.
I have since received from the managing editor of the Globe and Mail a full explanation of how the article came to appear in the form in which it did, and I have also received from the Canadian Press a statement which goes further to explain the circumstance of the article appearing as it did. I should like to read at once to the house these communications, because they completely exonerate Mr. Dingman in respect of the article referred to in so far as concerns the particular paragraph which was in quotation marks and to which I took exception.
The telegram received this morning from the managing editor of the Globe and Mail is as follows:
Right Hon. W. L. M. King,
Ottawa, Ont.
Quotation from your speech last Thursday for which you blame our Mr. Dingman in Commons last night was clipped from Canadian Press running report and inserted at our desk here Mr. Dingman having omitted that particular quote from his report. All Canadian newspapers have right' to rely and do rely on meticulous accuracy of house reports by Canadian Press which is official news gathering agency of Canadian newspapers. Mr. Dingman entirely ignorant of its insertion here and blameless for any variation from actual verbiage. Inasmuch as you denounced Dingman as having perpetrated a " false and perverted report, a very wilfully false and perverted report having regard to all the circumstances " I feel sure your sense of fairness will prompt you to
exonerate him in the same place from which you made the accusation. I have been in touch with Canadian Press executive and Canadian Press is issuing its apology for the paragraph in question which the Ololie and Mail in pursuance of its policy of unfailingly rectifying any error or injustice in its columns will glady carry in Wednesday's late edition and then through Thursday's early editions these early editions having gone to press to-night prior to m.v being able to straighten out this tangle.
Respectfully,
E. George Smith, Managing Editor, The Globe and Mail.
This morning I received from Mr. Carnegie, the superintendent of the Canadian Press at Ottawa, the following letter:
April 5, 1939.
Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
My dear Mr. Prime Minister:
In the body of The Canadian Press running report of your speech on international affairs last Thursday was a paragraph quoting you as follows:
"I cannot accept the view of some that regardless of circumstances this country must say here and now that Canada is prepared to support any action that may be decided upon by the government at Westminster."
As I have explained to you-
I should have mentioned that Mr. Carnegie also came to my office last night and immediately made an explanation to me.
-the same quotation appeared in the Globe and Mail's report to which you directed attention in the House of Commons last night. Evidently the Globe and Mail lifted the quotation from The Canadian Press report and incorporated it in its own report.
Later when the text of your speech was available The Canadian Press carried your exact words in this connection. You will note in the morning papers we express our regret.
You will realize summarizing a running report of a lengthy speech provides some margin of error and I think it is a tribute to the excellence of our parliamentary reportorial staff that the errors are so rare.
Most of our members used the textual excerpts of this and other portions of your speech we put out when we received the text including the Globe and Mail itself.
With kind regards,
Sincerely yours,
R. K. Carnegie, Ottawa Superintendent.
These two communications fully explain, I think, the circumstances in which the paragraph to which I took exception came to be inserted in Mr. Dingman's dispatch to the Toronto Globe and Mail. They were circumstances of which I had no knowledge whatever. Had I had any knowledge of them I
Royal Seals

should certainly not have spoken as I did. Let me say that I think the Globe and Mail has done all that possibly could be expected in the way of seeking to rectify the mistake. I think also The Canadian Press has done all that it possibly could in the way of rectifying the mistake. I should like on my part to do all I possibly can to remove from Mr. Dingman's mind any sense of injustice or wrong that he may feel has been done him by words of mine, occasioned as they were in the circumstances that are now known to the house. I need not say that in the light of the situation as it appeared from the article itself I felt that it was desirable, in the interest of the privileges of parliament, to make the remarks I did; but had I known of the circumstances I certainly should not have said what I did in reference to Mr. Dingman. I exonerate him completely, as have both the Globe and Mail and the The Canadian Press. I would say further that I do not think that either the Globe and Mail or The Canadian Press intentionally sought to alter the meaning of what I said, or in any way to misrepresent my position. I certainly did not wish to misrepresent Mr. Dingman's position. I wholly withdraw what I said in reference to him, and, as I have just said, I regret sincerely that he should have been occasioned feelings of injustice in reference to a matter in which he was wholly innocent, just as I myself regret the circumstances which caused me to feel a sense of injustice, and occasioned the necessity of making the remarks I did in this house last night.

subtopic: ISSUE OF ROYAL INSTRUMENTS AND ORDERS AND REGULATIONS WITH RESPECT THERETO

speechtext:
Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 76, to make provision for the sealing of royal instruments.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is intended to serve a double purpose, the first of which arises as a result of the prospective visit to Canada of His Majesty the King. During his majesty's presence in Canada under existing laws and practice it would not be possible to issue royal instruments under the great seal or the signet. This bill makes provision for passing such instruments under the great seal of Canada, of course in relation to Canadian affairs; for instance, in connection with giving full powers for the signature of treaties, and so forth. These are royal instruments, and the great seal has to be used.

subtopic: ISSUE OF ROYAL INSTRUMENTS AND ORDERS AND REGULATIONS WITH RESPECT THERETO
speechtext: Titles?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ISSUE OF ROYAL INSTRUMENTS AND ORDERS AND REGULATIONS WITH RESPECT THERETO
speechtext: No, not titles. That is done without so many instruments.

subtopic: ISSUE OF ROYAL INSTRUMENTS AND ORDERS AND REGULATIONS WITH RESPECT THERETO
speechtext: Oh no; they are laid on the table beside your plate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ISSUE OF ROYAL INSTRUMENTS AND ORDERS AND REGULATIONS WITH RESPECT THERETO
speechtext:
The second purpose is to make provision for Canadian royal seals for use in Canadian matters. This is for instance, for exequaturs, leave of absence to the governor general, and matters of the

Questions
kind. This will be permanent. The present bill is designed to enable Canadian transactions involving the use of royal seals to be subjected in form as well as in substance to the direct control of responsible Canadian ministers.	.

subtopic: ISSUE OF ROYAL INSTRUMENTS AND ORDERS AND REGULATIONS WITH RESPECT THERETO
speechtext: Does it include as well the use of the royal signet?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ISSUE OF ROYAL INSTRUMENTS AND ORDERS AND REGULATIONS WITH RESPECT THERETO
speechtext: Yes; not the royal signet as used in the United Kingdom.

subtopic: ISSUE OF ROYAL INSTRUMENTS AND ORDERS AND REGULATIONS WITH RESPECT THERETO
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt, but it is still used in the United Kingdom with regard to some Canadian affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ISSUE OF ROYAL INSTRUMENTS AND ORDERS AND REGULATIONS WITH RESPECT THERETO
speechtext:
This will not necessarily dispense with that. I think when the bill is distributed my hon. friend will see that the whole procedure will now be under the control of Canada. The great seal of Canada will be used, or another seal or signet may be used, but under the instructions of the Canadian parliament.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it has been suggested by the dairy council that it would be helpful if an advisory committee, composed of nominees of the dairy interests and perhaps one or two of the officials of the department, 7X492-165^

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT

speechtext:
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure making provision for a percentage deduction from all grain marketed in the spring wheat area, and making available other sums required for the purposes of the proposed act; to provide assistance to farmers in emergent conditions by making provision for an acreage payment, with provision also for the appointment and assignment of officials, auditors or employees.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution is the twin resolution of order No. 17 standing in my name on to-day's order paper, and having to do with the cooperative marketing of wheat. With the permission of the house I should like to apply my remarks at this
time to both resolutions; it will make unnecessary a second speech with regard to the other. The two are so closely allied that it is almost impossible to discuss the one without discussing the other.
The resolutions have to do with the marketing of wheat. Earlier in the session someone in the house said that every time I had spoken during the session I spoke with regard to wheat. He was somewhat critical of the fact that I had not addressed the house more frequently on other matters which have to do with agriculture. Here is one of the outstanding reasons why it has been necessary to discuss wheat rather frequently during this and other sessions. In my opinion many things have been done in connection with wheat in the last eight or ten years which have not been sound in principle. What has been done from time to time in connection with the marketing of wheat has made it very difficult to apply to the problem of the marketing of other farm products the principles which have been applied to the marketing of our main farm product, wheat. This being so, it has been necessary from time to time to discuss ways and means of so changing our policy in relation to wheat as to make it possible to apply to the marketing of other farm products the principles which have been applied to the marketing of wheat.
In this connection the report of the royal grain inquiry commission, 1938, the preparation of which required a period of two years, makes certain comments with regard to the policies followed in connection with the marketing of wheat. Hon. members will remember that this was a one-man commission; and at page 189 of the report the commissioner states:
I am therefore of the opinion that under what may be called normal conditions-open markets in the United Kingdom, a fair relationship between world supply and import demand, and no danger clouds on the immediate horizon- the government should remain out of the grain trade, and our wheat should be marketed by means of the futures market system (under proper supervision), and encouragement given to the creation of cooperative marketing associations, or pools. The government's activities should, I think, be confined, under these conditions, to such helpful action as I have already indicated and such as I shall refer to presently: trade agreements, assistance to commercial and economic research, to the gathering of information, to promotional services, etc.
Then with regard to this general recommendation, he states further on page 194:
For all these reasons (and notwithstanding the adverse considerations to which I have referred in relation to government boards) I do not feel that I can suggest the immediate dissolution of the Canadian wheat board. There

In the meantime I can think of nothing better to suggest than that the board be maintained to meet any situation which may arise.
These recommendations have to do with what might be called our permanent policy and the emergent policy which was to apply at least to the year 1938. In order that we may have before us what apparently was in the mind of the commissioner in relation to pools, I should like to read this further paragraph from page 182 of the report:
Our policy should then be the continuation of the futures trading market at Winnipeg and the encouragement of the building up of producers' cooperative marketing societies, organized and conducted in a manner approaching, in so far as practicable, the organization and business methods of the Australian pools to which reference has been made and which have been in successful operation for many years. I nave in mind pools organized on a flexible, voluntary basis, not necessarily of great size, selling in line with market conditions, and operating overseas "with the trade and not against it" as was said in reference to the Australian pools. Such pools should, in my opinion, make use of the futures market, not for speculation, as by long buying, but for hedging purposes such as the securing of a price, "when prices look attractive" as was said in 1924 by the manager of the Alberta pool; or again "to accommodate the buyer" as was also said on that occasion, care being taken in such last case to avoid speculation.

speechtext: Did that recommendation only have to do with normal conditions?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
I read the recommendation with regard to normal conditions. It was suggested that the wheat board be continued last year for the purpose of dealing with the situation, and the commissioner did not know how long in addition to last year it would be required. In order to place this matter before the house in the manner I desire, and before going on with a discussion of the wheat matter itself, I think it is of the utmost importance that we should lay down at this time-probably it was important that it should have been done even earlier-the general policy having to do with the marketing of farm products and the encouragement of agriculture generally.
I think it goes without saying that agriculture in Canada has been going through a most difficult period during the last eight or ten years. These difficulties have not all had to do with the marketing of wheat. There have been difficulties in connection with agriculture in other directions. I repeat that one of the main objectives which I have in mind in presenting this matter to the house at this 
time is to place before hon. members some sound principles upon which we may build in reestablishing agriculture generally across Canada. In order to get the true picture as to why' we have the present legislation, in order to explain the conditions under which it has operated and why it has operated in the way it has, I should like to place on Hansard some quotations from the remarks of two hon. gentlemen who presented this question to the house in 1935 when the present wheat board act was placed upon the statute book of this country.
The Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, then leader of the government, speaking on the grain board bill which was introduced in 1935, made certain statements setting forth his views with regard to the matter of wheat marketing and conditions generally related thereto. In moving the second reading of this bill he stated, as reported at page 3562 of Hansard of 1935:
Need I remind the house that the reason wheat plays so large a part in the economic life of Canada is that it is a product which is more readily converted into new wealth than any other resource upon which we can have reliance to take care of our adverse trade balances and to increase the purchasing power of our people. I need hardly remind the house that when there is a favourable crop with a favourable market the railways have traffic and that when the railways have traffic employment on the railways is larger than it otherwise would be. I need hardly remind the house that in eastern Canada, whether it be Quebec, Ontario or any part of the country, the ability of the industrial population to produce in their factories and mills the requirements of the population west of the lakes depends entirely upon our ability to market our crop of wheat.
That expression, I think, is the well-considered opinion of all parties in this house, and it needs no further comment from me. Mr. Bennett then asked, as reported at page 3572 of Hansard of 1935:
Can the people of this country afford to see the wheat that plays so large a part in our economic life become the sport and play of what is called supply ancf demand at 38 cents a bushel ?
Mr. Bennett answered this question at page 3577 of Hansard, toward the end of his speech, in these words:
The terms and provisions of the bill are short and simple. It provides for the marketing of the Canadian wheat crop through the channel I have indicated, and not through a private enterprise. It is to be done through a public board created by the Dominion of Canada.
Those words are clear and unmistakable. They state that the board is to handle all the wheat grown in Canada which goes into interprovincial and export trade.
Hon. J. L. Ralston, speaking in 1935 for the Liberal party, then the official opposition, on the grain bill of that year, which later

Farm Assistance-Acreage- Payment
became the wheat bill, and replying to Mr. Bennett, said, as reported at page 3581 of Hansard:
I do not believe that the people of the Dominion of Canada are favourable to a compulsory wheat board, to a board the constitution of which will mean that every wheat grower, every elevator man and everybody engaged in the wheat business must deal with the government agency and no one else. This matter of policy lias been discussed before not only in this house but throughout the country. The government has carried on with a voluntary system for five years as Mr. McFarland and the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited have been nothing more or less than a board conducting voluntary market operations. A man was entitled to sell or not sell to Mr. McFarland as he saw fit. I submit that so far as the western wheat grower is concerned that the voluntary system should be continued until there has been more opportunity to consider the matter. I do not believe the compulsory feature of this bill will meet with approval, either in the west, in the east or in this house.
There you have the issue clearly drawn between the two parties at that time in the house: one was for compulsion; the other was for a continuance of the voluntary system.
Following this discussion the bill went to a committee and returned with some amendments, and in the course of the discussion which took place when the bill came back to the committee of the whole, Colonel Ralston made this statement:
I submit that this is an emergent measure due to the situation in which we find ourselves, and to some extent perhaps an experiment, one which will have to be tried out in order that we may find out whether it is the best for all concerned.
May I say Mr. Speaker, that when this bill came back from the special committee to the committee of the whole house it was entitled the Wheat Board Act of 1935, and not the Grain Act of 1935. Colonel Ralston, after making the statement I have just quoted from Hansard, continued, on the same page:
Before this bill comes out of the committee, I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) who is in charge of the measure, should reconsider the proposal made to him in the committee and insert some clause in the bill to indicate its nature, namely, that it is an emergency measure; that it is for the purpose of dealing with the situation in which we find ourselves; that it is to bridge the gap; to provide, as suggested in the committee, that the bill should be in force for one year, giving the governor in council power _ to extend it for a second year and providing at the end of that second year that it should automatically lapse unless it is further extended by parliament. That is the feeling which I have with regard to this matter.
In those words Colonel Ralston expressed the opinion of the Liberal party as then represented in the House of Commons.
Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, speaking on the same occasion in reply to what Colonel
Ralston had said, after pointing out the changes which had been made before the bill received its third reading, made this statement, as reported at page 4273 of Hansard:
We have this bill which the committee accepted for the purpose of doing two things: one, taking care of the surplus accumulations of the wheat of this country at a time when the requirements of importing countries have been enormously reduced, as will be found from the returns, and the production has made no corresponding diminution; second, this year's crop is to flow into the channels of consumption by the methods I have mentioned: a fixed price, a sharing in subsequent profits, if any, and the purchase by the board directly from the producer.
Then, at page 4274 of Hansard, Mr. Bennett made this statement:
But over and above and beyond all else stands the fact that whatever may be said, the board must be amenable to the orders in council and direction and control of the government of the day.
It will be noted from these statements that certain departures were made from the announced policy regarding the nature of the proposed legislation between the time the bill was introduced and its final passing. The bill as it entered the house declared that all grain entering interprovincial or international trade was to be marketed through a government board. This would have declared the marketing of grain a government monopoly and would have forced out all others in the trade in a very short time. But when the bill became an act it provided for setting an initial price; it left the individual free to sell to whom he chose. It provided that grains other than wheat would be handled by the board only if it were decided to do so by order in council.
Representative speakers on both the government and the opposition side had agreed that the main objects of the legislation were to dispose in an orderly manner of the carryover which had accumulated, and, while that was being done, to provide farmers who were marketing new crops with the protection of a fixed price through a government board.
It had been further stated by the prime minister of the day, at more than one point in the discussions, that the actions of the board were subject to the will of council; to use his own words already quoted:	.
But over and above and beyond all else stands the fact that whatever may be said, the board must be amenable to the orders in council and direction and control of the government of the day.
When these undertakings were given, indicating that the legislation was to deal with a temporary condition, that it was not a permanent policy, and that even while it

Farm Assistance-Acreage Payment
was in force it was subject to the control of the government of the day, it passed the house unanimously.
I place this record on Hansard in order that the position may be quite clear in any discussion which may take place in regard to the actions of the government from that day to this, whether under the previous prime minister or the present Prime Minister.
The Wheat Board Act of 1936 went into operation in the summer months of 1935, and a board was appointed under this legislation. The board set an initial price for wheat of 874 cents a bushel, No. 1 northern, Fort William. The newly appointed board took over an accumulated surplus of 205,000,000 bushels of wheat from Mr. McFarland, who had been conducting stabilization activities in previous years. Between August of 1935 and December 3, 1935, the board purchased from the producers 102,766,855 bushels of wheat, and sold 12,577,668 bushels of wheat, leaving a further accumulated surplus of 90,000,000 bushels. So that on December 3, 1935, the McFarland board turned over to the Murray board 295,000,000 bushels of wheat, covered by grain and contracts. The Murray board proceeded to deal with the surplus of 205,000.000 bushels accumulated prior to 1935, and with the wheat taken from the producers in 1935, in exactly the manner intended by the understandings reached between Colonel Ralston and Mr. Bennett when speaking on the floor of the house. That is, the board proceeded to the orderly marketing of the 205.000,000 bushels of wheat which had been carried into that year from the previous crop years, proceeded to handle the sale of that wheat so as not to interfere with the marketing of the wheat then coming on the market in that crop year.
The board attempted to get rid1 of as much as possible of the accumulated surplus before the new crop came on the market in 1936 and after the bulk of the 1935 crop had been delivered by the farmer. The result was that the government paid, under the 874 cent price guarantee for the 1935 crop, $11,858.104 more for the wheat than it actually netted on the market after paying costs and storage.
The amount of wheat disposed of during the year was 254,000,000 bushels, which reduced the board's carry-over to 84,698,652 on July 31, 1936. The government in dealing with the producer in 1935-36, had a certain experience which, I think, is of interest in a discussion of this question. Colonel Ralston was right in 1935 in stating on the floor of the house that the majority of the farmers both east and west were opposed to the setting up of a govern-

ment monopoly in grain handling and marketing facilities. Had I had any doubts about that at the time he made the statement, they would have been absolutely removed by the actions of our farmers themselves during the marketing season of 1935. The price of wheat during the last three weeks of September and during October, 1935, was above, but only slightly above, the set price of 874 cents. At the end of any week it was never higher than 94-2 cents Fort William, and the lowest was 88-6 cents, which is only slightly above the 87J cent price. Actual closing prices at the end of each week were: 89-7; 94-2; 91-1; 94-2; 92-6; 90-2; 88-6 respectively. Prior to October 25 there had been delivered by the farmers 145,670,535 bushels of wheat.

Yes, for No. 1 northern. During these three weeks 4,000,000 bushels were delivered to the elevators by the farmers, of which quantity only 1,500,000 bushels were delivered to the board, while 2,500,000 bushels were delivered to the trade. This indicates that little more than one-third of the farmers were prepared to risk a loss of from four to five cents a bushel in order to support the idea that the government should market all the wheat through the wheat board.
During the period from the end of October, 1935, to the first of July, 1936, wheat, as I said, was below 874 cents a bushel, and all the wheat delivered during that period came to the board. In addition to all that was delivered to the elevators during that period, there was an amount of 19,000.000 bushels which had been placed in storage by

Farm Assistance-Acreage Payment
the farmers during the months of September and October, when the price was above 874 cents, which was passed over to the board at 874 cents during the period when wheat was below 871 cents.
The meaning of that is simply this, that of that quantity of wheat which was delivered when the price was above 871 cents and the farmer was holding the wheat under his own control, 19,000,000 bushels were turned over to the board after the price went below 871 cents and remained there. I recite these facts in order to point out that what Colonel Ralston and others said at the time the bill was being considered in the house, was in accordance with the facts as they knew them in relation to grain handling in western Canada. This experience was sufficient to convince the government-that is, the government o'f the present day-that farmers are not yet prepared to risk wheat with a government agency and take a flat price for it under all circumstances. If the choice is left and the government desire to handle all the wheat, then they can do so only by setting a price above the market and keeping it there. I think the figures prove that if the government do not at all times offer a better price than the market will bring, they will not get enough wheat to pay for the overhead cost of doing business, and that the act can function with participation as a possibility only so long as the farmers are absolutely sold on the idea of cooperation. It can function only when the world price is below the set price. Until the farmer has decided that he desires a cooperative set-up, such voluntary legislation can function only as a bonussetting piece of machinery. We paid a bonus to the extent of $6,182,453 in 1935. We paid that bonus to the farmers at the rate of about four cents a bushel on wheat delivered to the board in 1935, and in addition we paid $5,675,650 in carrying charges, mostly storage. I shall refer to that figure later on in a discussion I desire to carry on with regard to this method of marketing.
It was argued in 1936 and 1937 that the set price should be raised because the world price was rising. The government still adhered to the original intent of the act and maintained that an effort should be made to put the surplus into consumption and thus get rid of it rather than accumulate more. The government knew from the experience of the preceding year that unless we were prepared to advance the price periodically throughout the year, keeping it on a level with the world price, the government board would not function as part of the marketing
machinery for continuing delivery of the current crop. In order to avoid later confusion through having on our hands a small volume of wheat which those who actually follow a principle, even to the extent of great financial loss, had delivered, we stated that unless wheat dropped below 90 cents, the board would not take delivery of any wheat. We acted on the understanding reached at the end of the discussions of 1935 when the Wheat Board Act became law, and determined this action by order in council. I believe that in doing so, once having decided that we could not advance beyond 874 cents, we saved a group of farmers who would follow a principle to the bitter end even if they had to take a loss. We saved them from a loss which they certainly would have suffered had they depended upon the legislation for marketing their crop that year. We knew from the experience of the wheat pools, and have since had it corroborated by the experience of 1938, that it is most difficult to adjust your set price on a falling market if you have advanced it on a rising market. One of the difficulties experienced by the pools in 1928, 1929 and 1930 was the fact that they had set a comparatively high price during the period of high and rising prices, and they found it most difficult to reduce that price in the years when the price itself was falling.
I have come to the conclusion that to ignore the so-called law of supply and demand, as Mr. Bennett said his government intended to do when they brought in the first bill in 1935, will eventually wreck any system that can be devised, by loading the system with an enormous surplus or by giving it an enormous deficit. Wheat went up to an average of $1.22 a bushel for No. 1 northern at Fort William in 1936-37 and to an average of $1.31 a bushel in 1937-38. In order, then, to have been in a position to take delivery of wheat during that period the government would have had to be periodically advancing the price from 874 cents until wheat reached a price which was above that at which wheat was being sold from time to time, in order to assure that the government would get delivery of a sufficient volume to be worth while.

The farmer, therefore, did not need the assistance of the government to market his crop to advantage. The carryover in Canada was reduced to 23,411,171 bushels by July 31, 1938, which is as low as it could be reduced in any year, in view of the wheat distributed here and there in elevators and in farmers' bins throughout the country. It reduced the surplus to 23,411,171 bushels; and the farmers were able, in the two years during which that surplus was being reduced, to market their wheat at a higher price than they had experienced for many years previously.
Then the board was continued during the year 1937-38 to assist in the distribution of seed grain. That is, there was a comparatively small bushelage of wheat in the hands of the board at the end of the crop year 1936-37; that small bushelage was made available for supplying wheat to farmers for seed in the spring of 1938, and the board was continued in order to take care of that and of the winding up of the business which had been done.
The Turgeon report was brought down in the spring of 1938. During all this period of activity the Turgeon commission had been sitting. For all these reasons (and notwithstanding the adverse considerations to which I have referred in relation to government boards) I do not feel that I can suggest the immediate dissolution of the Canadian wheat board.

On February 16 last, as reported at page 1035 of Hansard, I pointed out that the 1935 act operated merely to pay a bonus, and it required the experience of 1938 to prove how inequitable such a bonus could be. Those with good crops were drawing as high as from $3 to $7 an acre from the treasury on wheat which had already brought them a gross return of S10 to $20 an acre.
In the fall of last year Premier Bracken of Manitoba called a conference in Winnipeg to discuss agricultural problems. This conference met from December 12 to 15, 1938. The conference was well constituted and
admirably conducted, and published a comprehensive report of the papers presented. That in view of the present international position with reference to the marketing of wheat, and of the importance of the wheat industry within the general economy of the Dominion of Canada.
And of the necessity of the continuance of protection for western wheat growers, at least to the extent of the protection afforded to them during the crop year 1938-39, and pending the determination of a permanent western wheat and agricultural program to which this committee is devoting and proposes continuously to devote its study and attention.
The dominion government be requested to establish as its wheat policy for the crop year 1939-40:
(1)	The continuance of the *wheat board for 1939-40.
(2)	The setting of a guaranteed price for
wheat of at least 80 cents for No. 1 Northern, basis Fort William.	.
In addition to the foregoing the committee considered the possibility of subsidiary assistance, as follows:
The committee, while it believes that the wheat industry by reason of its very nature and of the position which it occupies in the national economy, requires specialized consideration, is also aware of the difference between the problem of protection for the wheat industry, the problem of that limited class of farmers who grow coarse grains for sale, and the problem of those farmers who by reason of drought or other calamity suffer a total or partial crop failure.
In view of what may evolve as the particular needs of the twro last named classes, the committee submits to the government for consideration the extension to those classes of some system of reasonable assistance and in particular ask the dominion government to consider some subsidiary assistance by way of a crop insurance plan or some other method to assure all farmers an improved minimum maintenance income.

Professor E. C. Hope was invited to address the conference which met in Winnipeg, on the subject of what the price of wheat means to western farmers. Professor Hope is connected with the university of Saskatchewan, in the province where the greatest amount of wheat is grown; he makes economic studies in connection with agricultural matters. He said:
One more word I might say about the present system of bonus this year. This year it may cost the federal government $60,000,000-we don't know-but whatever it is, personally I think it is about the most unfair kind of bonus you can possibly give western agriculture, because it gives a definite bonus to the man with a big crop, and nothing to the man with a crop failure. There is no bonus on coarse grains. The farmer with no crop is out of luck. If there is no change in policy by next spring we will have a shift to increased wheat acreage. If I were a farmer I would plant more wheat next year. Why? Because oats are 15 cents a bushel and wheat is between 58 and 60 cents a bushel.
He was speaking of the prices on the farm, not the prices at Fort William.
A farmer would be dull if he did not react in this manner; and this is exactly what he is thinking of right now. To make the bonus fair, if it should be necessary in another year, it should be based on the total acres of crop land.
This is the opinion of the man who has been paid by both the government of Saskatchewan and the federal government to study this question from an economic point of view.
To make the bonus fair, if it should be necessary in another year, it should be based on the total acres of crop land. In western Canada we have approximately 60.000,000 acres broken up-summer fallow, oats, barley and all crops combined. One dollar an acre on all land broken gives no special emphasis on either oats, barley or wheat. It gives equal emphasis to all, and if wheat is sold at, let us say, a market price of 40 cents the total cost would be the same this year and probably some wheat would be fed. This wheat is not fed at 60 cents.

At a dollar an acre basis it wouldn't cost any more money to the government of Canada. But bonusing the price of wheat prevents the very thing you are trying to do, it does not help to feed any of that surplus. As long as the farmer can get 60 cents for wheat he will not feed wheat to hogs.
This, let me repeat, is the opinion of Professor Hope, who is connected with the agricultural school at the university of Saskatchewan, in the very centre of the wheat growing area, Of course he takes the simplest way possible of setting up an acreage bonus; he says, "If you get a dollar for every acre broken up in western Canada, it will amount to exactly the sum it is estimated will be lost this year as a result of handling the crop under the plan followed in the past."
The government of Saskatchewan, the greatest wheat growing province in Canada, had a full study made of the matter. I think I can say without much fear of contradiction that the minister of agriculture of that province is easily the outstanding agricultural authority of western Canada. He was one of the ablest officials of the department which I now have the honour to administer before I took over this department, and before he became minister of agriculture of the province of Saskatchewan. He was so moved by the inequalities resulting from the payments made last year under the 80 cents set price which resulted in the expenditure of this large amount of money, that he had a man appointed to make a complete study of those inequalities; and I think the facts as I placed them on Hansard on February 16 have convinced everyone who read them that the inequalities under that system could not properly be continued. Knowing as we do that so many districts with low yields got such small consideration and so many districts with high yields got a great deal of consideration, it would be difficult for a government to continue a policy which would maintain all the inequalities of the system that we had during the last year.
Some criticism has been made to the effect that the government should have known, before setting the 80 cent price, that these inequalities would develop. Well, I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the government did know that some inequalities were sure to develop, as soon as we were operating on a falling price market, with an unequal crop. There was some indication of that at the time the price was set, but any indications that there were then were accentuated by what happened from that time on. We knew as a matter of fact when we set the price last year that we would take a loss. We did not anticipate a loss as great as may develop, but we were prepared to take some

loss to assist the farmers who had come into the difficulties of a world surplus immediately after eight years of crop failure. Rust and grasshoppers added to the inequalities, even after that price had been set.
I still think, Mr. Speaker, that the government took the only move that was open to it, with the legislation which was on the statute book, when that price had to be set in the year 1938.
Immediately the price was set I was asked by the government to make a personal study of the problem with a view to evolving a plan which would remove the weaknesses of the present system, and possibly put into effect as soon as possible the recommendations of the Turgeon commission. I personally drove over a considerable part of the wheat area, during harvest. And while people were thankful for the bonus where there was wheat in quantity, I heard nothing but criticism of the inequalities of a system which paid $4.50 an acre to the man with thirty bushels to the acre, and nothing to the man with two bushels, who had to keep his seed. That is, he had nothing to sell, when he had only two bushels to the acre, whereas the man with thirty bushels to the acre was able to secure from the sale of his grain, even at the market price, $15 an acre, and he got an additional $4.50 an acre from the treasury. The Saskatchewan government collected records of the whole area, and forwarded them to the government here. These records proved to me conclusively that the inequalities of the system could not be continued. I so stated to the house on February 16. Now, I ask hon. members, what do the records show with regard to the handling of the 1938 crop, in relation to what could have happened had we had a crop similar to that of, say, 1928?

We in western Canada are suffering from exactly the same difficulties as those which other countries where wheat has been sown have suffered from, periodically, over the years gone by.
I think it is time we recognized a few of the obvious facts when we are dealing with this question in the house. Wheat of a kind can be grown almost anywhere in the world; therefore you cannot force your wheat upon anyone. There are a great many foods which can be used as substitutes for wheat in a diet. I believe Germany has proven that conclusively in recent years. Wheat is not a luxury food. It must be eaten in considerable quantities by working people, if it is to be consumed at all. It must therefore be available at a competitive price. There is one lesson which we should have learned from our experience with stabilization which has apparently been forgotten. Terminal, transfer and all types of elevators. Three large milling corporations operate eighty per cent of the milling capacity of Great Britain, and there are buyers from other countries desiring to buy wheat in Canada. When there is an open market, the companies which have the wheat in. store in Canada are anxious to dispose of it at a reasonable price and thus save carrying charges. That is, once they have taken delivery of wheat and have it in their storage facilities, they are naturally anxious to sell it at a price which will get them out of the transaction. Therefore, they become active agencies to sell the wheat. The millers are anxious to make sure that they will have a proper proportion of our strong wheat to put in their mix. There is, accordingly, constant competition between buyer and seller. There is a group anxious to find markets, and there is another group anxious to establish stores under their control. That is the condition under the open market, and the tendency of the system is to get the best possible price even though the competition causes constant variations. It is true that the best price may not prevail at a time when the farmer is delivering his greatest volume of wheat, but the tendency is for prices to take a higher level under competition than they do under other methods.
But let us examine the condition when the government has all the wheat. Because the price was above the market in 1938, the government took delivery of practically all the wheat. As there was no chance of the set price being reached, the farmer rushed all the wheat to the government as soon as possible and got his money. The wheat was then in store at the government's expense. The elevator operator has not the same reason to be an agent for its sale. I do not say that he is not taking part in the sale of our grain, but he has not the same reason to be active. The usual charge for storing is a
[(Mr. Gardiner.]
cent a bushel a month. Therefore, the elevator operators have no special reason to be anxious about markets. A cent a bushel a month will pay the average cost of carrying grain. I may say that the wheat board is not paying that much for spreading wheat, say from December or September into May; it is paying considerably less than that, but the usual charge to the producer is a cent a bushel a month.
The buyer knows who has all the wheat; he knows it is the government of Canada, and he has no reason to be anxious about his supply. All the wheat is under one ownership. Since the government is meeting the carrying charges, he tends to buy wheat as he needs it. If he is a wise business man-and these importers all are-he will come and get it at the bottom rather than at the top of the market. The result is that we carry the grain at our expense for both seller and buyer, and the price levels off at the bottom of the market rather than at the top or in the middle. I venture to say that Canada has lost from five to ten cents a bushel on her wheat this year through having it all in the possession of the government.
With these facts in mind, and many others which I have not time to cover, it would be impossible for the government to continue to sit indefinitely in the middle of the grain trade-it may do so for a time in order to deal with an emergency-taking delivery of grain from producers, paying a bushelage bonus on it, storing it until the trade requires it and then handing it back to them to be exported. That makes of us wood haulers and bottle washers for the importing countries. To my mind, those are not the best circumstances under which to handle the grain crop of the farmers of this country.
It is evident that Mr. Justice Turgeon recognized the importance of retaining the competitive element in the trade. Not only did he recommend that the government get out of the grain business, but he also recommended our encouraging pools rather than a pool. He even suggested that these pools should operate on the market much as other dealers. Having decided not to set a price of 80 cents a bushel at this time and having determined to ensure a certain return per acre to the wheat farmer, it became necessary for the government to consider setting up a system which had some chance of being permanent and which at the same time would tend to carry the farmer over his difficult years. This is the only method by which the industry can be rendered permanent on a basis which will make homes upon farms in western Canada a possibility.

It has been decided to make use of these facts in setting up a system of assistance which will be helpful in retaining the agricultural industry in the western provinces.
About eighty per cent of the wheat is usually delivered to the elevators between August 1 and December 1 of each year.
The average 320-acre farm in western Canada has eighty acres of wheat grown upon it. The average 480-acre farm may have as much as 200 acres of wheat. In some parts of the west the 320-acre farm is the family unit, and in others-it is necessary to have 480 acres in order to farm to advantage.

After having given full consideration to all these matters the government proposes to pay an acreage bonus for 1939-40 not to exceed $1 an acre in townships where the average yield is from eleven to fifteen bushels an acre; of $2 an acre in townships where the average yield is from six to ten bushels an acre; and of $2.50 an acre in townships where the average yield is from nothing to five bushels an acre, provided wheat is not above 70 cents a bushel If it is above 70 cents on an average from* August 1 to December 1, there will be a deduction of one-tenth for every cent that it is above 70 cents, which will result in the assistance disappearing at SO cents a bushel.
This will be true of all townships in municipalities with over a five-bushel average. Those with five bushels or less, which will take in most persons up to six or seven bushels provided it is a crop failure year, will obtain the assistance no matter what the price may be.
If a man has no wheat to sell, it makes no difference what the price is. If he has a crop failure, as he had in 1937 or 1931, the payment is $2.50 per acre on half his cultivated acreage with a maximum acreage upon which payment can be made of 200 acres and a minimum of 100 acres and the payment will be made irrespective of what the price of wheat is.

speechtext:
There are certain conditions set out in the legislation. In this proposed legislation, 1939-40 is declared an emergency year, and this system will apply

to 1939-40. The reason being that we have just come through seven or eight crop failures in many parts of the west where the farmers did not get the advantage of the 80 cent price this year because they had no wheat. So we propose in the bill that this particular year shall be called an emergency year. From that time on, the assistance will be given on the same basis, with the provision that the government can vary the 10 cent range which controls the amount of the payment and thus keep control of the cost to the government.
To illustrate how this compares with the assistance given under the 80 cent guarantee given in 1938, perhaps I might give some figures. On a half section of land, all under cultivation, assuming that, the farmer had No. 1 northern wheat and sold at the average which might have been secured between the first of August and the first of December last; assuming, further, that the farmer grew about eighty acres of wheat on the half section; and assuming, still further, that farmer retained two bushels to the acre for seed, the farmer with fifteen bushels to the acre and receiving 80 cents a bushel Fort William under the guaranteed price could have sold his wheat for $676 on the half section.
Under the proposed plan, assuming that the wheat is No. 1 northern, he could have received, at the average price prevailing, $520 for his wheat, and he could have received, as an acreage bonus, $160, giving him a gross return of $680 from wheat sale and government assistance. If I may be permitted I should like to place on Hansard a table which will show the comparative amounts that could have been obtained in 1938 under the 80 cent price, with the amounts that could have been obtained had this system been applied to 1938 in the manner I have indicated, with the average price as it was from August to December at 65 cents a bushel on the market.

speechtext:
In the particular case I have described it would be $160, and it would be $160 in every case from there down to eleven bushels; from eleven bushels down to five bushels the amount would be $2 an acre on half the acreage, and from 5 bushels down, it would be $2.50 on half the acreage.

Farm Assistance-Acreage Payment
The object of this plan is to set up a permanent policy for western agriculture. It gives the farmer assistance at the time he needs it. The man with 20 bushels an acre would be in a position to sell 18 bushels and therefore would receive, on the same basis, $720. That is, he would obtain that as his selling price in any case, because of having grown wheat without government assistance at all. The man with 19 bushels would get $680, or the same as the man with 15 bushels obtained after receiving government assistance. It figures out in this way: even after the man with 15 bushels has received assistance, he gets the same amount as the man who had 19 bushels and had no assistance; and most of those receiving 16, 17 and 18 would find themselves in townships averaging 15, and therefore would share in the acreage payments in most years. If, therefore, you take the table as I have outlined it, and as I shall place it on Hansard, and compare the amounts which would go to the farmers operating under these conditions, taking at the same time the figures above-I have given five above 15 acres- you will get some idea of the way in which the system will work in practice. If one applied the system to those operating larger farms, and therefore receiving payments up to 200 acres, one would find that all those who had 10 bushels or under would have received more under the new plan for the 1938 crop up to 400 acres of cultivated acreage than they did receive, provided they had had 200 acres cropped to wheat. Those from 11 up would have received slightly less until they got to 15 and still less up to 20. In other words, under the system which is proposed, farmers who have up to 15 bushels an acre and are farming a half-section would get more money under this system up to 15 bushels an acre than they did get under the 80 cent set price last year, in years when there was an emergency or when there was a crop failure; and so far as those farming three-quarters of a section are concerned and who would have probably 400 acres under cultivation, they would obtain more up to 10 bushels an acre. Beyond that, they would have got more under the 80 cent price.
To indicate the weakness of the policy under which the 80 cent payment is maintained as compared with this, one has only to point out that those who grew 20 bushels to the acre could have obtained last year $10 an acre for wheat; those with 30 bushels to the acre would have obtained $15; and those with 40 bushels to the acre would have received $20, without assistance.
It is difficult to justify the payment of another $3 to the first man, more difficult
to justify the payment of another $4 to the second, and even more difficult to justify the payment of $6 to the third man. It is doubtful if anyone could justify asking the people of Canada to make this latter payment, and if it were done it might endanger any method which might be set up for bringing assistance to the grain-growing industry as such in western Canada or obtaining suitable assistance in time of crop failures. This is a matter that should be given careful consideration in dealing with this question. If we are to set up a system which will tend to become permanent we must be reasonable in what we are suggesting. We must make it appeal to the reason of people outside of western Canada as well as to people in the west, and it seems to me that it would be rather difficult, even in a year like last year, to justify paying $6 an acre more out of the treasury of Canada to a man who was already able to get $20 an acre for the wheat he sold off that particular land. If we attempted to make that a permanent policy in Canada to apply to difficult years, I think we should have a great deal of difficulty in keeping it on the statute books. moment ago, a man farming a half-section and having 15 bushels to the acre, would have been 65 cents a bushel. This year, of course, he is naturally complaining, because without a set price he would have had to take in the neighbourhood of 40 cents a bushel for that same wheat. Up to 400 cultivated acres and all those with less than 11 bushels per acre would have received more than they would have received with the 80 cent set price. On all the acreages lower than 320 which come under the act the advantage in favour of the new plan would be even greater.
Someone might criticize the payments on the higher yields, say from 12 to 15 bushels, but I think they can be justified on the ground that a charge is being made of one per cent of all grain which comes to the terminals. That is, the proposal in the measure is to take one per cent of all the grain that comes to the terminals, sell that grain, put the money in a fund, and then if necessary contribute to that fund from the treasury in very much the same way as we do now in our schemes for setting up pension payments to employees, or in any scheme for the provision of insurance payments to unemployed under an unemployment insurance scheme.

We have not up to date, but we are proposing one from time to time, and it would have those features.
The main criticism to date is that we have fixed the price at 60 cents. I wish to make it plain that this proposal does not set a fixed price for wheat. We have not fixed a price for wheat at all if this proposal goes into effect. We have fixed, by this and the proposed cooperative marketing measure, the twin measure I spoke of a moment ago, which is suggested in order No. 17, an assured amount which farmers can get per acre, which in most cases is a little more than enough to cover cost of production as figured by the university of Saskatchewan. By adopting the two measures I have indicated, in the one, the cooperative marketing measure, a readiness to guarantee a sound system of pooling conducted by producers and those with facilities who are not producers-

speechtext:
To the four western
provinces. The adoption of this system will assure to farmers a means of securing an advance on their grain every year up to 60 cents a bushel. They are assured by the measure proposed in this resolution the additional amount necessary to cover the recognized cost of production in emergency years, but no assurance is given in connection with other years, because it is presumed that they will get this in the ordinary marketing of the crop.
If hon. members have any doubts as to the liberality of such a plan as the measure proposed, they have only to compare the returns per acre with any hail insurance scheme we have had in western Canada, whether under a private corporation or under governments or municipal organizations.

speechtext:
What
about frost?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Frost might come in in an emergency year, and rust, but not crop failures caused by these.
If I were asked how we arrived at 60 cents, which was the question asked a little while ago in regard to the 80 cents, I should say that in only two years out of the last forty-nine, for which we have the records, has wheat been below 60 cents on an average throughout the year, and in one of those years it was only one-fifth of a cent below. I read in the debates of 1935, in the speech of the then leader of the government, that up to that time in only one year out of four hundred had that been the case. But I checked for myself the last forty-nine years, and I find there were only two years during that period in which the average price was below 60 cents. In one it was 59-8 cents, and in the other it was 54 cents and a fraction. Those years were 1932 and 1933.
We therefore think that the government is taking little if any risk in a scheme of this kind as far as the 60 cent advance is concerned. In taking that position we are doing exactly what elevator companies have done over the last fifty years. You could always take a load of wheat to an elevator in western Canada and get an advance on it. In the years when prices were advancing you could get up to 60 per cent of the market price, and some farmers got even more than that. In years when the price was going down you could get probably 50 per cent or 40 per

Farm Assistance-Acreage Payment
cent of the price on the day you took it to the elevator, and leave your wheat there and sell it whenever you liked. So that as far as this system is concerned the government has worked out the point at which we think we would be experiencing the same measure of security as elevator companies have had in the past in dealing with a different situation, and it is believed that over a term of years we would take no loss in connection with the 60 cent advance thus made.
All the money which is paid out in order to help farmers under a plan of this kind is paid out after careful consideration by the government of the existing circumstances, and a decision made by the governor in council. And that decision would be made, not before the crop is harvested, but in the month of December, when everyone knows the facts. In addition to that, the payments would not be made in one lump sum, but 60 per cent would be paid in December and 40 per cent in the following March, thus making it possible for farmers who were in that position to maintain themselves on the payments made to them through the early part of the winter at a standard higher than the standard now provided by any system of relief given in any western province or anywhere else for that matter.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: There would be only two periods of payment, would there?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext:
Just two periods of payment. It provides for a payment in March, at a time when we in this house and every legislature in the three prairie provinces are being appealed to to provide seed in the spring. In other words, by this system we would be doing two things. We would be attempting to take western Canada out of the position into which the western farmer has been forced in regard to financing ever since western Canada was opened up, namely, the selling of all our crop, collecting all our money when we threshed the crop, having all our creditors sitting on our doorstep the day we thresh to collect everything they can collect, and then finding ourselves trying to live through the remainder of the year in the hope that we shall have a crop next year with which to pay debts incurred during the year. Under this system, if it can be applied in western Canada, and I think it can, we would give the western farmer in his periods of difficulty the opportunity of doing what farmers have done in every other part of Canada and any part of the world where weather conditions have been sufficiently constant, that is, pay his way as he goes along
by selling his produce from day to day, week to week, and month to month, thus being able to pay his bills as they come in. We in western Canada have been on a different basis. We have experienced I think more difficulty because of the credit system we have been forced by circumstances to follow than through any other cause. It seems to me that the system just outlined would tend to get us away from this difficulty, and I believe any help which this house can give by laying down that system would be action in the right direction.
To sum up, I would say that the outstanding features of the acreage insurance plan are these:
1.	The township is used as the unit to determine yield, thus avoiding dependence on individual declarations, and also leaving some room to benefit from individual effort, while giving no encouragement to farming poor land.
2.	Wheat is used only as a means to determine the crop yield; the payment is made on half the cultivated acreage up to 200 acres, whatever is grown on it.
3.	Because of the payments I have described, encouragement is given to summer fallowing, grass growing and mixed farming.
4.	Because of the limitations referred to, the half-section and three-quarter-section home units are encouraged rather than the large farm.
5.	A charge of one per cent of all the grain which goes to the terminals forms part of a fund, the remainder of which, when necessary is provided from the treasury. This is the same principle as would probably be followed in any unemployment insurance plan which might be adopted.
6.	The year 1939 is declared an emergency year in the bill. The government must first declare any succeeding year an emergency year before the month of December.
7.	Acreage payments will be made in an emergency year of $1 an acre on half the cultivated acreage in all townships with an average yield of from 11 to 15 bushels per acre, of S2 an acre in all townships with an average yield of from 6 to 10 bushels per acre, and of $2.50 an acre in all townships with an average yield of from 0 to 5 bushels per acre.
8.	These payments will be made in 1930-40 in full if the average market price of wheat from August to December is not more than 70 cents. If the market price is more than 70 cents, one-tenth will be taken off the above

Farm Assistance-Acreage Payment
amounts for every cent that it is more than 70 cents. When it reaches 80 cents no amount will be payable under this part.
9.	In succeeding years the government will set the governing 10 cent controlling maximum and minimum.
10.	In years of crop failure caused by grasshoppers or drought, of proportions which constitute a national calamity, payments will be made in municipalities with an average of 5 bushels or under at the rate of $2.50 an acre on half the cultivated acreage, irrespective of whether it is an emergency year and irrespective of price.
11.	If this plan had been in effect in 1938 those residing in townships with an average yield from 15 bushels down, farming half a section of land with the average wheat acreage, and those with 400 acres under cultivation with 10 bushels or less, could have received more from the sale of their wheat and acreage payment than they received from the 80 cent price.
12.	As a permanent policy this measure would function with the act to encourage cooperative marketing of wheat, which guarantees a 60 cent advance. This makes it possible for any individual to assure himself an advance payment which with the acreage payment guarantees him a minimum return from his cash crop.
13.	It is impossible to estimate costs of production on a cost per bushel basis because of the variation in yield. It is comparatively easy to estimate costs on an acreage basis. The university of Saskatchewan have estimated these costs at from $6 to $8 per acre.
14.	The minimum acreage cost guaranteed under this bill on a basis of wheat usually grown on a half section of land runs from $5 an acre, where the yield is under 6 bushels, to over $8 an acre where the yield is under 16 bushels.
15.	With the bill as drawn and functioning with the act to encourage cooperative marketing of wheat, the farmer can still draw in addition through participation certificates or sale on the open market if the price permits another 10 cents a bushel before the provisions reducing the possible acreage payments begin to operate.
16.	With the two bills functioning a half section farmer with 80 acres sown to wheat, living in an area with a 15 cent charge in store Fort William, an area with an average yield of 15 bushels to the acre, could have obtained an amount equal to 65 cents a

bushel at his local elevator for No. 1 northern wheat. Those with 10 bushels to the acre could have obtained an amount equal to $1 a bushel.
17.	It has been considered wise in view of general conditions following a period of poor crops and the accumulated surplus on hand from last year to continue the wheat board. It is proposed that the wheat board function in the same manner as a central selling agency would if the cooperative wheat marketing act had been in effect. This if accepted will result in all the advantages of the above plan being immediately available and experience being gained which when normal conditions return will make the complete plan easily applicable.

speechtext: If I may ask a question, has the minister any estimate to give the house as to what this might have cost the country, in round figures, if it had been in operation during the past year?

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT

Our present estimate is that even if the worst conditions we have ever experienced had prevailed it could not have cost more than about $30,000,000; and that in the ordinary year it would cost somewhere between $10,000,000 and $15,000,000. The greatest amount it could cost would be half what the existing scheme may cost this year under present conditions. I may add that in order to get that last figure you would have to take in the cost of relief, which will amount to some $12,000,000, in addition to the amount paid out already in connection with wheat.
In conclusion, then, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer again to what I said in the beginning. I bring this measure before the house for the purpose of calling attention to a situation which has existed in western Canada for many years and to efforts which have been made to cope with the situation, with a view to bringing before the house during this session other measures that are now either on the order paper in the form of resolutions or that will be on the order paper to-morrow in that form, for dealing with agriculture in other parts of Canada. Before bringing down these measures I should like if possible to have this house establish a principle that we can apply in connection with our agricultural problems throughout Canada, If that is done the same principle can be followed in dealing with the problems of the dairy industry, the live stock industry, the fruit industry and

The Royal Assent
other branches of agriculture across this country. I believe that if we can establish a principle of that kind during this session we have at least started to give Canada an agricultural policy which will lift agriculture out of some of the difficulties it is experiencing from one end of the dominion to the other. It is with that end in view that I bring this measure before the house.
I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that I gave an undertaking to many of the western men who left last night and the night before, that after making this speech I would delay further discussion if possible until they returned. With the permission of the house, therefore, I will move the adjournment of the debate.

subtopic: CREATION OF DEFENCE PURCHASING BOARD TO ENTER INTO CONTRACTS FOR MUNITIONS, EQUIPMENT, MATERIALS AND SUPPLIES

speechtext: The house resumed consideration, in committee of Bill No. 38, to establish a defence purchasing board-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver) -Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: CREATION OF DEFENCE PURCHASING BOARD TO ENTER INTO CONTRACTS FOR MUNITIONS, EQUIPMENT, MATERIALS AND SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Before royal assent I was referring to a question asked last Wednesday, when we last considered this bill, in connection with Bristol aeroplane engines. While it is scarcely pertinent to the discussion of this particular bill, I should like to amplify the statement I made the other day. I referred to prices paid by the British air ministry to Bristol Aeroplane Company, Limited, for Bristol engines. I have since learned that under the provisions of the agreement between the air ministry and Bristol Aeroplane Company, Limited, the former is precluded from disclosing the prices paid by the air ministry for Bristol engines. I have also been since informed that there is good reason to believe that the relations between the air ministry and the company already mentioned are of a confidential nature in this respect, being virtually that of a qualified partnership, and that it is deemed inadvisable by the air ministry to disclose either the prices paid by them for these engines or other details of the relations at the present time.
In view of the situation and with the fullest recognition of the air ministry's position, I wish to amplify my previous statement to the house. The Department of National Defence purchases Bristol engines at prices quoted by the Bristol Aeroplane Company, Limited, which are " subject to reduction, if any, following consultation with the British air ministry." The department maintains a liaison officer in the British air ministry. Among other duties, he has to seek the greatest possible benefit from the air ministry's advice and assistance

in checking these prices. On April 1, 1939, the liaison officer forwarded the following information to the department:
Air ministiy arrive at price by negotiations based technical cost, investigation overhead charges after making provision for capital clause liability, machine tools, etc. As we include accessories in our demand and air ministry purchase only bare engines from manufacturer we cannot get same price as air ministry. On the whole believed we get reasonable approximate price definitely below foreign price. Air ministry under agreement not to reveal their price but always willing to examine our price and say whether considered fair and reasonable which would give a definite indication that prices approximate those of air ministry.
I can only add that the Department of National Defence does take advantage of and deeply appreciates the cooperation and assistance extended to us by the British air ministry in this and other directions.
While I am on my feet I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 3, 1939, which cast some doubt upon the value of Bristol engines when operated under Canadian conditions. In this connection I should like to quote the following memorandum which was received from the chief of the air staff:
For the past three winters the Department of National Defence has carried out winter flying tests on Bristol engines, in collaboration with the British air ministry. These tests have been made under all weather conditions, and Canada was chosen because of the severe conditions. Results have been entirely satisfactory.
The question of icing of carbureters is not peculiar to Bristol engines, but is largely a question of installation, and the report of the loss of the Cavalier has naturally resulted in a review of the engine installation of all types of aircraft. It is not anticipated that any difficulties will be met which cannot be overcome.
I thought I owed it to the committee to give this amplified statement.
